name: Zero-Based Budgeting
title: Zero-Based Budgeting
answer: Zero-based budgeting is a planning method in which every cost line starts at zero for each new budget cycle and must be justified by a stated purpose, a cost driver, and an expected outcome. It sits inside forecasting and planning work, where it contrasts with incremental budgeting that rolls last year's base forward with adjustments. In practice it covers operating expenses, discretionary spend, project portfolios, and sometimes capital requests, though many organizations apply it selectively rather than to every account. The method forces a link between spending and activity, so it is used when leaders need to reallocate resources, absorb a shock, or reset a cost base after a merger or restructuring.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Zero-based budgeting runs on the same financial data foundation as other planning processes, including the general ledger, chart of accounts, cost centers, vendor records, and headcount data. Planning platforms, enterprise resource planning systems, and spreadsheets hold the budget models, while data warehouses and extract, transform, load pipelines feed actuals and commitments into them. AI and machine learning components may sit alongside these systems for anomaly detection, cost driver clustering, forecast reconciliation, and scenario simulation, but they depend on clean, timely, and well documented source data. Access controls, version history, and a single source of truth for actuals are practical requirements because the method asks managers to rebuild every number from evidence.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work usually begins with a decision package for each activity, service, or project, describing what it delivers, what it costs, and what would happen if it were reduced or stopped. Teams map costs to drivers such as transaction volume, headcount, square footage, or service level, then rank packages by strategic fit, risk, and return. Finance and business partners review the ranked list, test assumptions against historical actuals, and set the funded level for the next period. The cycle repeats with variance analysis, so a zero-based budget is not a one-time exercise but a recurring planning discipline that can be supported by driver-based models and rolling forecasts.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in zero-based budgeting center on data provenance, auditability, and fair treatment of the activities being funded. Governance practice assigns an owner, a source, and a version history to every assumption, allocation rule, and decision package so that internal audit and regulators can trace how a number was built. Common risks include managers gaming the ranking, hidden cross-subsidies between departments, and cuts that damage compliance, safety, or long-term capability because the model undervalues them. Where AI assists with scoring or anomaly detection, teams document training data, monitor for bias, and keep a human decision point for material funding choices.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Zero-based budgeting is moving toward continuous and driver-based forms, where funding is revisited as conditions change rather than once a year. AI and machine learning are being applied to cost driver discovery, package scoring, natural language summaries, and scenario generation, which can shorten the review cycle and surface overlooked trade-offs. The main constraint is not model capability but data quality, change management, and the willingness of managers to defend spend from first principles. Over time the method is likely to blend with rolling forecasts and activity-based costing, with automation handling the mechanics and people focusing on prioritization and risk.
